patient.chief_complaint: Sudden onset left-sided weakness and inability to move left arm and leg
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Khalid Al-Rashidi is a 63-year-old right-handed Arab man with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, active tobacco use, and known three-vessel coronary artery disease (managed medically, last angiogram 4 years ago) who was brought to the emergency department by his wife after sudden-onset left-sided weakness. The patient and his wife report that he was watching television at home at 14:20 when he suddenly dropped his cup of tea with his left hand and was unable to raise his left arm. He then tried to stand and found his left leg would not support his weight. His wife, who was present throughout, confirms he had no symptoms before this moment. She called emergency services immediately. EMS arrived at 14:35, documented left hemiplegia, left facial droop, and rightward gaze deviation. Field glucose was 168 mg/dL. A prehospital stroke alert was activated and the patient arrived in the ED at 14:58. The patient denies headache, loss of consciousness, preceding visual changes, chest pain, palpitations, nausea, vomiting, or seizure activity. He has no prior history of stroke or TIA. He endorses increased tobacco use over the past year (approximately one pack per day) and acknowledges his blood pressure has not been well-controlled despite two antihypertensive agents — he has not seen his primary care physician in 14 months. He also admits to missing several doses of his aspirin and clopidogrel over the past two weeks because of a gastrointestinal upset. His wife confirms no new medications, herbal supplements, or illicit substances. Time of last known well is established at 14:20, approximately 38 minutes before ED arrival. He speaks primarily Arabic; his son, who arrived shortly after EMS, is assisting with interpretation.

results.title: 2019 AHA/ASA Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
results.authors: Powers WJ, Rabinstein AA, et al.
results.key_finding: IV alteplase (0.9 mg/kg) recommended within 4.5 hours of symptom onset in eligible patients. Mechanical thrombectomy recommended for LVO up to 24 hours in select patients by DAWN/DEFUSE-3 criteria. Non-contrast CT head is the first imaging step to exclude hemorrhage.

results.title: Stenting versus Aggressive Medical Therapy for Intracranial Arterial Stenosis (SAMMPRIS Trial)
results.key_finding: Aggressive medical management (aspirin, clopidogrel dual antiplatelet for 90 days, risk factor control) was superior to percutaneous transluminal angioplasty and stenting (PTAS) for secondary prevention in symptomatic intracranial atherosclerosis with 70-99% stenosis.

results.title: Prevalence and mechanisms of stroke in intracranial atherosclerotic disease
results.key_finding: Intracranial atherosclerotic disease (ICAD) is a leading cause of ischemic stroke in Asian, African American, and Hispanic populations; mechanisms include in situ thrombosis, artery-to-artery embolism, and perforator occlusion. Aggressive risk factor modification is the cornerstone of secondary prevention.

interactions: Aspirin 81 mg daily: Increased bleeding risk with concurrent thrombolysis; aspirin is not a contraindication to IV alteplase per AHA/ASA guidelines but should be held 24 hours after alteplase administration.
Clopidogrel 75 mg daily: Antiplatelet agent — not a contraindication to IV alteplase at standard antiplatelet dosing; monitor for bleeding; hold 24 hours post-alteplase.
contraindications: Dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel): Not a contraindication to IV alteplase per AHA/ASA 2019 guidelines when used at standard antiplatelet doses. Full therapeutic anticoagulation would constitute a contraindication, but antiplatelet therapy does not.
INR 1.0, PTT 28 s — no coagulopathy contraindication to thrombolysis.
No recent major surgery reported; no active bleeding.
warnings: Patient on DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel) — bleeding risk is modestly increased with thrombolysis; acceptable per guidelines if clinical benefit outweighs risk
Lisinopril: Monitor for orolingual angioedema — ACE inhibitors increase angioedema risk with alteplase; observe closely post-infusion
Metformin: Hold if contrast studies anticipated (CTA); no direct interaction with alteplase
Monitor blood pressure: Must maintain BP <185/110 mmHg before tPA and <180/105 mmHg for 24 hours after
alternatives: Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg IV single bolus (non-inferior to alteplase per AcT trial; simpler bridging-to-thrombectomy profile)

sequence_constraints.reason: Non-contrast head CT must exclude intracranial hemorrhage before IV thrombolysis is considered.
Glucose, INR/PTT, and platelet count must be reviewed before IV thrombolysis to exclude hypoglycemia mimic and coagulopathy.

critical_actions: Establish time of last known well (14:20) and apply NIHSS to confirm acute treatment eligibility
Obtain non-contrast CT head FIRST to exclude intracranial hemorrhage before any thrombolytic decision
Achieve door-to-needle time <60 minutes given onset-to-door time of 38 minutes (still within 4.5-hour tPA window)
Maintain blood pressure <185/110 mmHg before IV tPA and <180/105 mmHg for 24 hours after
Verify glucose to exclude hypoglycemia as stroke mimic
Proceed to mechanical thrombectomy evaluation given right MCA M1 LVO on CTA (NIHSS 14, ASPECTS 9)
Monitor for ACE inhibitor (lisinopril) — associated orolingual angioedema following alteplase infusion
Initiate 24-hour Holter and prolonged cardiac monitoring to exclude occult paroxysmal AF
Begin secondary prevention with high-intensity statin (LDL target <70 mg/dL) and optimize diabetes control
Recognize mildly elevated troponin as likely demand/neurogenic injury rather than primary ACS given sinus rhythm, no wall motion abnormality on echo, and flat troponin trajectory
contraindicated_actions: Do not administer IV tPA before non-contrast CT excludes intracranial hemorrhage
Do not lower blood pressure aggressively below 140/90 mmHg in the acute phase outside tPA window — risks worsening ischemic penumbra
Do not delay non-contrast CT imaging for additional labs or evaluation in a stroke alert
Do not assume mildly elevated troponin indicates primary ACS without echo and serial trending — neurogenic troponin elevation is common in acute stroke
Do not discontinue dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel) abruptly without considering ICAD secondary prevention protocol
Do not give IV tPA if INR >1.7, platelet count <100,000, recent major surgery, or other contraindications listed in AHA/ASA 2019 guidelines
key_reasoning_points: Right MCA territory stroke causes contralateral (left-sided) motor and sensory deficits; gaze deviates toward the lesion (rightward) — cortical gaze preference ipsilateral to stroke side
Absence of aphasia in right MCA territory stroke is expected in right-handed patients with right-hemisphere (non-dominant) infarcts; left hemispatial neglect is the expected cortical sign

Intracranial atherosclerotic disease (ICAD) is the most common cause of ischemic stroke globally and the dominant mechanism in Arab, Asian, and African American populations with heavy vascular risk factor burden

Mild troponin elevation in acute ischemic stroke commonly reflects neurogenic (Takotsubo-pattern) cardiac injury from catecholamine surge — absence of wall motion abnormality and flat serial troponins distinguish this from primary ACS

TOAST classification by mechanism — large-artery atherosclerosis — requires >50% stenosis or occlusion of a major brain artery with compatible syndrome; ICAD on CTA with eccentric calcification satisfies this
Normal sinus rhythm on ECG and 24h Holter does not exclude paroxysmal AF; prolonged monitoring (30-day event monitor) is recommended if mechanism remains uncertain after initial workup
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=amyloid_PET): Amyloid PET has no role in acute ischemic stroke evaluation
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=DaTscan): Dopamine transporter SPECT has no role in acute ischemic stroke workup
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=FDG_PET): FDG-PET is not part of routine acute ischemic stroke workup

red_herrings.data_point: Troponin I mildly elevated at 0.08 ng/mL on admission labs
red_herrings.intended_effect: Prompt premature diagnosis of concurrent acute MI and divert workup toward primary ACS evaluation, potentially delaying stroke reperfusion
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mildly elevated troponin in acute stroke is commonly neurogenic (demand ischemia or Takotsubo-pattern catecholamine surge); serial troponin is flat and echo shows no wall motion abnormality, excluding primary ACS as the dominant diagnosis

metadata.real_seed_note: Extensive PMC literature search conducted (searched for right MCA LAA male CC-BY case reports); no qualifying CC-BY PMC case report with confirmed right MCA large-artery atherosclerosis in an Arab male patient was identified. Case authored de novo as a clinically authentic confirmed acute ischemic stroke presentation, consistent with project policy for real-seeded generation when no verifiable CC-BY seed is available. Demographics, mechanism, territory, and tool outputs reflect published epidemiology of ICAD in Arab/Middle Eastern populations.
metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward — acute onset left hemiplegia + rightward gaze deviation in a 63-year-old Arab male with heavy vascular risk burden; right MCA M1 near-complete occlusion on CTA with underlying ICAD changes; mildly elevated troponin serves as a realistic red herring (neurogenic) but does not obscure the primary diagnosis.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Single diagnostic chain — right MCA ICAD with LVO; straightforward presentation with clear laterality; one red herring (neurogenic troponin) grounded in initial labs.
